breakfast.name: Qaimaq (Cream) with Naan Bread
breakfast.description: Traditional Afghan breakfast featuring rich clotted cream served with fresh warm naan bread, often accompanied by honey and Afghan tea
instructions: Heat milk and cream in a heavy-bottomed pot over low heat
Add cardamom seeds and saffron strands
Let simmer for 10-12 minutes until cream layer forms on top
Gently skim the cream (qaimaq) into a serving bowl
Warm ghee in a pan and brush onto naan breads
Arrange naan on a platter
Serve qaimaq with naan, drizzle with honey
Serve alongside Afghan chai (cardamom tea)
breakfast.notes: Qaimaq requires patience - the creamier the milk, the better the result
breakfast.fun_fact: Afghan cardamom tea (chai) is often called 'chai-e-siyah' (black tea) or 'chai-e-shir' (tea with milk). Cardamom was historically one of Afghanistan's major spice exports along the Silk Road.
alternatives: Greek yogurt instead of qaimaq for lighter version
Honey instead of ghee for vegetarian preference
Store-bought pita bread instead of fresh naan

breakfast.name: Bolani (Herb-Filled Flatbread)
breakfast.description: A stuffed flatbread with leeks and herbs, served with yogurt and dal. This street food is especially popular during Ramadan and is a hearty Afghan breakfast staple.
ingredients: 3 leeks (white and light green parts), chopped
instructions: Mix flour and salt; add warm water gradually to form soft dough
Knead for 10 minutes until smooth; cover and rest 20 minutes
Heat ghee in a pan; add cumin and coriander seeds
Add chopped leeks; cook until softened (about 5 minutes)
Stir in cilantro, mint, turmeric, and black pepper; cool filling
Divide dough into 6 equal portions; roll each into thin circle
Place 2-3 tbsp filling on one half of each dough circle
Fold dough over filling, seal edges by pressing with fork
Heat oil in a skillet over medium-high heat
Cook bolani until golden brown on both sides (2-3 minutes per side)
Serve hot with yogurt and dal (lentil soup)
breakfast.notes: Can also be filled with potatoes and spinach. Fresh herbs are essential for authentic flavor.
breakfast.fun_fact: Bolani is so important in Afghan culture that it's served at celebrations, weddings, and as a quick street food. The herb-filled version represents the abundance of Afghan gardens.
alternatives: Spinach instead of leeks for vegetarian variation
Butter instead of ghee for different flavor profile
Whole wheat flour for healthier version

lunch.name: Qabuli Pulao (Chickpea and Carrot Rice)
lunch.description: Afghanistan's national dish - fragrant rice cooked with caramelized carrots, chickpeas, and meat, topped with yogurt and fresh herbs. Each grain of rice is separate and flavored with cardamom and bay leaves.
ingredients: 1 lb lamb or beef, cut into chunks
3 large carrots, julienned or cut into thin sticks
Salt and black pepper to taste
Fresh cilantro and mint for garnish
instructions: Soak chickpeas overnight; drain before cooking
Heat 1 tbsp ghee in a pot; brown meat chunks on all sides; set aside
In same pot, add remaining ghee and onions; cook until golden
Add cardamom, bay leaves, cinnamon, cloves, and cumin
Return meat to pot; add chickpeas and water
Simmer for 20 minutes until chickpeas are tender
In a separate pan, heat 1 tbsp ghee; fry carrots until edges caramelize (8-10 minutes)
Season carrots with salt and pepper; set aside
Rinse rice under cold water until water runs clear
In a pot, bring salted water to boil (ratio: 2 parts water to 1 part rice)
Add rice and cardamom pods; boil 6-8 minutes until partially cooked
Drain rice, reserving some cardamom
Layer meat mixture, then rice, then caramelized carrots in serving dish
Drizzle remaining ghee on top
Cover and let rest 5 minutes
Serve with yogurt, fresh herbs, and carrot garnish
lunch.notes: The key to perfect pulao is using long-grain basmati rice and the caramelized carrots. Quality ghee is essential.
lunch.fun_fact: Qabuli Pulao is served at all Afghan celebrations and is the official national dish. The name 'Qabuli' refers to the chickpeas, which are a major protein source in Afghan cuisine. It was perfected during the time of the Afghan kings.
alternatives: Butter instead of ghee for creamier texture
Canned chickpeas instead of dried to save time
Chicken instead of lamb for lighter version

lunch.name: Shorba (Afghan Stew)
lunch.description: A warming, hearty stew featuring lamb or beef with chickpeas, beans, and vegetables in a fragrant broth. Often served with rice or flatbread.
ingredients: Salt and black pepper to taste
instructions: Heat oil in a large pot; brown meat on all sides
Add onions and cook until softened
Add tomato paste and stir for 2 minutes
Add turmeric, coriander, and cumin; toast for 1 minute
Pour in water or broth; bring to boil
Add cardamom, cinnamon, and bay leaves
Reduce heat and simmer for 20 minutes
Add potatoes, carrots, chickpeas, and beans
Simmer for additional 30-40 minutes until meat is tender
Season with salt and pepper to taste
Remove cardamom pods, cinnamon stick, and bay leaves
Garnish with fresh cilantro
Serve with rice pilaf or flatbread
lunch.notes: Best served the next day after flavors have melded together.
lunch.fun_fact: Shorba is comfort food across all regions of Afghanistan and is traditionally served during winter months and at family gatherings. The variety of legumes shows the importance of plant-based proteins in Afghan cuisine.
alternatives: Chicken instead of lamb for lighter option
Red lentils instead of chickpeas for vegetarian version
Tomato sauce instead of paste for brothier consistency

dinner.name: Kofta (Afghan Meatballs)
dinner.description: Aromatic meatballs made with ground lamb or beef, onions, herbs, and spices. Served with yogurt sauce and rice, kofta is a dinner staple across Afghanistan.
instructions: In a bowl, combine ground meat with onion, cilantro, mint, garlic, and ginger
Add cumin, coriander, turmeric, egg, and breadcrumbs
Mix gently until combined but not overworked
Form into oval-shaped meatballs about 2 inches long
Heat oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat
Cook kofta in batches, turning occasionally for 8-10 minutes until browned
Mix yogurt with lemon juice and serve as dipping sauce
Serve kofta with rice, yogurt, and fresh bread
dinner.notes: Don't overwork the meat mixture or kofta will become tough. The mixture should be just combined.
dinner.fun_fact: Kofta traces its origins back to Persian cuisine but has become quintessentially Afghan. The combination of fresh herbs gives it a uniquely Afghan flavor that distinguishes it from Persian versions.
alternatives: Beef instead of lamb for leaner option
Chickpeas instead of meat for vegetarian version
Yogurt-mint sauce instead of plain yogurt

dinner.name: Haft Mewa (Seven Fruits Stew)
dinner.description: A complex, fragrant stew combining meat with seven different dried fruits - apricots, raisins, prunes, dates, pomegranate, barberries, and quince. Sweet, savory, and aromatic.
ingredients: 2 cups quince puree or canned quince paste
Salt and black pepper to taste
2 tbsp sugar (optional, if fruits not sweet enough)
instructions: Heat oil in a large pot; brown meat on all sides; set aside
In same pot, add onions and cook until softened
Return meat to pot
Add cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, and bay leaves; toast for 1 minute
Dissolve saffron in warm water and add to pot
Pour in remaining water/broth and bring to boil
Reduce heat and simmer for 30 minutes covered
Add apricots, raisins, prunes, dates, and quince paste
Simmer for additional 40-45 minutes
Add pomegranate seeds and barberries in last 5 minutes
Season with salt, pepper, and sugar if needed
Serve over rice pilaf
dinner.notes: The balance of sweet and savory is key - adjust sugar based on fruit sweetness. Quality barberries make a significant difference.
dinner.fun_fact: Haft Mewa ('seven fruits') is traditionally served during Nowruz (Persian New Year) celebrations to symbolize abundance and prosperity. Each fruit has symbolic meaning in Afghan culture.
alternatives: Chicken instead of lamb for lighter version
Dried cranberries instead of barberries
Apple puree instead of quince paste

snacks.name: Sambusa (Fried Pastry Pockets)
snacks.description: Crispy fried pastry triangles filled with spiced potatoes, chickpeas, or meat. A beloved street food and appetizer throughout Afghanistan.
instructions: Make dough: Mix flour and salt; add oil and water gradually
Knead until smooth dough forms; cover and rest 20 minutes
Make filling: Heat oil in a pan; cook onion and garlic
Add ginger, cumin, coriander, and turmeric
Add mashed potatoes and chickpeas; mix well
Stir in cilantro; season with salt and pepper; cool
Roll out dough into thin sheet; cut into squares
Place 1 tbsp filling on each square
Fold into triangle, sealing edges firmly
Heat oil for frying (350-375°F)
Fry sambusas in batches until golden brown and crispy (2-3 minutes)
Drain on paper towels
Serve hot with tamarind chutney or mint yogurt sauce
snacks.notes: Keep folded sambusas covered with damp cloth until frying to prevent drying out. Oil temperature is critical for crispiness.
snacks.fun_fact: Sambusa is believed to have originated in Central Asia and Persia, but Afghan sambus has become famous for its crispy pastry exterior and flavorful filling. They're sold by street vendors throughout Kabul.
alternatives: Beef instead of potatoes for meat-filled version
Spinach instead of potatoes for vegetarian variation
Spring roll wrappers instead of homemade dough for convenience

snacks.name: Pakora (Vegetable Fritters)
snacks.description: Crispy vegetable fritters made with chickpea flour batter and fried until golden. Served with mint chutney or yogurt sauce.
instructions: Mix chickpea flour with turmeric, chili powder, cumin, and salt
Gradually add water to make thick batter
Let batter rest for 5 minutes
Coat potato, onion, spinach with batter
Heat oil to 350-375°F
Carefully place battered vegetables in oil
Fry in batches for 2-3 minutes per side until golden and crispy
Drain on paper towels
Serve hot with mint chutney
snacks.notes: Make sure batter is thick enough to coat vegetables but thin enough to fry properly.
snacks.fun_fact: Pakora is popular street food in Afghanistan and is often served with Afghan chai or tea. The chickpea flour gives it a nutritious protein boost.
alternatives: Sweet potato instead of regular potato
Bell peppers instead of spinach
Yogurt-based dipping sauce instead of chutney

desserts.name: Kheer (Rice Pudding)
desserts.description: A creamy, aromatic rice pudding made with milk, rice, and flavored with cardamom and pistachios. Served chilled or warm.
instructions: Rinse rice under cold water; drain
Heat ghee in a heavy-bottomed pot
Toast rice in ghee for 2 minutes, stirring constantly
Add milk and bring to boil
Reduce heat and simmer, stirring occasionally, for 30 minutes
Add sugar, cardamom pods, and saffron
Continue simmering for 10-15 minutes until rice is very tender and milk reduces
The kheer should be creamy and coating consistency
Remove cardamom pods
Sprinkle with cinnamon powder
Garnish with pistachios and almonds
Serve warm or chilled
desserts.notes: Constant stirring prevents rice from sticking to the bottom. The pudding thickens as it cools.
desserts.fun_fact: Kheer is served during special occasions and celebrations in Afghanistan. The use of saffron indicates this is a dessert for important guests, as saffron is expensive and highly valued.
alternatives: Regular white rice instead of basmati for cost savings
Milk powder mixed with water instead of fresh milk
Cashews instead of pistachios

desserts.name: Firnee (Ground Rice Pudding)
desserts.description: A silky smooth, delicate pudding made from ground rice, flavored with cardamom and rose water, and topped with pistachios and almonds.
ingredients: 1 cup rice flour or ground rice
instructions: Heat ghee in a heavy-bottomed pot
Add rice flour and roast for 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly
Gradually add milk while stirring to avoid lumps
Keep stirring to incorporate milk smoothly
Add sugar, cardamom pods, and saffron
Bring to gentle boil, then reduce heat
Simmer for 15-20 minutes, stirring frequently
The mixture should thicken and become smooth
Add rose water and salt
Pour into individual serving bowls
Garnish with pistachios and almonds
Serve chilled
desserts.notes: Firnee should be smooth and silky. Constant stirring is essential to prevent lumps.
desserts.fun_fact: Firnee is often served on special Islamic occasions. The rose water used is traditionally from Isfahan, Iran, which has the finest rose-water production in the region.
alternatives: Cornstarch instead of rice flour for thicker pudding
Heavy cream instead of milk for richer version
Orange blossom water instead of rose water

nonAlcoholicDrinks.name: Afghan Chai (Cardamom Tea)
nonAlcoholicDrinks.description: A fragrant black tea infused with cardamom, often served with milk. This is the national beverage of Afghanistan and is central to Afghan hospitality.
ingredients: 4 tbsp black tea leaves (or 4 tea bags)
instructions: Bring water to boil in a kettle
Add cardamom pods and crushed them slightly
Add black tea leaves and let steep for 3-4 minutes
Strain tea into cups or a serving pot
In a separate pot, warm milk with sugar or honey
Pour tea into cups, filling 3/4 full
Top with warm milk
Add pinch of salt
Stir and serve immediately
nonAlcoholicDrinks.notes: Afghan chai is always prepared fresh when guests arrive. The cardamom should be crushed just before brewing for best flavor.
nonAlcoholicDrinks.fun_fact: Afghan hospitality mandates serving chai to guests. The saying goes: 'A guest without chai is like a party without music.' Chai is served in small handleless cups called 'piyala.'
alternatives: Green tea instead of black tea for lighter version
Honey instead of sugar
Ginger instead of cardamom for warming spice

nonAlcoholicDrinks.name: Sharbat (Afghan Fruit Drink)
nonAlcoholicDrinks.description: A refreshing fruit drink made from pomegranate, grape, or other fruits, diluted with water and served chilled. Traditional summer drink during hot Afghan summers.
instructions: Pour pomegranate juice into a pitcher
Add water and stir well
Add sugar and lemon juice
Stir until sugar dissolves
Add pinch of salt
Chill in refrigerator
Serve over ice
Garnish with fresh mint and orange slices
Stir well before each serving
nonAlcoholicDrinks.notes: Can be made with other fruit juices such as grape, apple, or apricot.
nonAlcoholicDrinks.fun_fact: Sharbat is served at weddings and celebrations. During Ramadan, it's especially popular as it helps break the fast with quick energy and hydration.
alternatives: Grape juice instead of pomegranate
Honey instead of sugar
Lemonade base for different flavor

alcoholicDrinks.name: Arak (Anise-Flavored Spirit)
alcoholicDrinks.description: A traditional clear spirit distilled from grapes and flavored with anise seeds. Often drunk as an aperitif before meals in Afghan celebrations.
instructions: Place anise, fennel, and caraway seeds in a glass jar
Pour spirit over seeds
Cover jar and let steep for 2-3 weeks
Strain through cheesecloth
Store in glass bottles
Serve at room temperature in small glasses
Traditionally served with water, which turns the drink cloudy white
alcoholicDrinks.notes: Arak should be sipped slowly, not gulped. The drink turns milky white when diluted with water (called 'louching').
alcoholicDrinks.fun_fact: Arak is traditional to Middle Eastern and Afghan culture for centuries. In Afghanistan, it's served during celebrations but has become less common due to Islamic traditions.
alternatives: Ouzo instead for Greek version
Pastis for French version
Raki for Turkish version
